[原文翻譯：We learned yesterday that a judge has approved a $32 billion lawsuit to proceed, accusing Apple Photos' facial recognition feature of violating state privacy law.

Although the two companies' practices sit at opposite ends of the privacy spectrum, this case has been conflated with Meta's use of facial recognition. In allowing the case to proceed, the court fundamentally misunderstands how the feature works...

The Earlier Lawsuit Against Meta

To understand this correctly, we need to first look at a facial recognition lawsuit against Meta that dates back to 2015.

Because that facial recognition runs on Meta's servers, and Meta can identify those faces, the company did break the law, and rightly was forced to settle the claim for $650 million.

Apple is now being sued under the same Illinois law — the Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) — which states that companies cannot collect biometric data without consent.

Apple's Approach Is Fundamentally Different

There is a huge problem with this allegation: Apple absolutely does not collect biometric data to power the face recognition feature in its Photos app. As Apple pointed out in a machine learning research paper in 2021, the recognition algorithms run entirely on-device.

Beyond that, all the iPhone does is tell you 'these photos all look like the same person' — it has no idea who that person is. The only person who can name them is the iPhone's user.

Apple's privacy policy for photos reflects this same point.

What baffles me is that this lawsuit has been bouncing around the legal system for six years, when a few minutes of research would have made it obvious that the lawsuit's allegations are plainly wrong.

Courts and legislators should be actively praising Apple's approach to privacy, not conflating it with the practices of privacy-destroying companies like Meta.

This is yet another example of courts and legislators completely failing to understand the technology they are attempting to regulate. The most obvious example, of course, is the matter of end-to-end encryption. Multiple countries have threatened or attempted to ban end-to-end encryption, yet they have absolutely no idea how encryption actually works.

I certainly understand that judges and politicians cannot be experts in every field. But they have access to experts, and it boggles my mind that lawsuits and draft legislation can go for years without anyone pointing out these fundamental errors.
